episodes.194006: Severe thunderstorms developed along a convergence boundary that stretched from Limon to Sterling. The storms produce hail up to an inch and a half in diameter, winds to 60 mph, two landspout tornadoes and flash flooding.
episodes.194113: Pre-frontal and sea breeze induced storms moved offshore of the local Atlantic coast and produced strong wind gusts.
episodes.194126: A cold front stalled across the Coastal Plain during the afternoon of August 19th. As this occurred, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the Coastal Plain just out ahead of this front and gradually tracked eastwards into the northern coastal waters and Pamlico Sound on the evening of August 19th. A few of these storms brought damaging wind gusts to the waters from Pamlico Sound north.
episodes.194251: An active week of severe weather unfolded across the Northern Rockies from August 18th through the 21st. Subtle waves lifting through a southwesterly flow aloft just west of an upper level ridge combined with ample surface heating and shear to result in multiple rounds of severe weather, most notably on August 19th when a line of strong thunderstorms lifted northward across the plains and adjacent areas.
episodes.194301: A slow moving storm and heavy downpour resulted in urban flooding within the city of Pierre. The COOP observer in town recorded 2.84 inches of rain, while the ASOS at the Airport recorded 1.68 inches during a 2 hour span. Pooling of water resulted in both streets and sidewalks under water in portions of the city.
episodes.194319: A frontal system brought rounds of showers and thunderstorms on the evening of the 19th. Heavy rainfall of 2-3��� fell near Lake Winnipesaukee in New Hampshire, resulting in localized flash flooding.
episodes.194417: An isolated thunderstorm over Wheatland Country produced a severe wind gust. Elsewhere, the downward momentum of some rain showers, combined with gap flow across the Livingston area, resulted in a 76 mph wind gust.
episodes.194449: Severe thunderstorms produced large hail on August 19.
episodes.194732: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the Brevard and Treasure Coasts.
episodes.194794: A thunderstorm became severe in northwest Crook County and tracked east-southeast across the county. The storm produced hail up to baseball size and wind gusts to 80 mph. The Devils Tower area sustained significant damage to trees and property. The storm also became tornadic for a brief period over the Bear Lodge Mountains, south of Alva. Many trees were either uprooted or snapped in half along the path, but no property was impacted by the tornado.
episodes.194801: A severe storm tracked out of northeast Wyoming and across the northern Black Hills area to the west central South Dakota plains during the evening hours. The storm produced large hail and heavy rain across the area. Flash flooding was noted in Deadwood later in the evening as two to five inches of rain fell in about three hours from several thunderstorms.
episodes.194808: A thunderstorm became severe over the northern Black Hills area, producing large hail and gusty winds over portions of the area.
episodes.195202: A shortwave moved across Wyoming and brought severe thunderstorms to portions of central Wyoming. A 60 mph wind gust was reported at the Lander airport in Fremont County. In Johnson County, quarter size hail was reported to the southeast of Linch.
episodes.195281: Sea breeze convection turned severe in coastal South Carolina.
episodes.195540: August 20th was characterized by a relative downturn in available moisture as some drier air worked in from the northwest. With the lack of upper level support, the higher terrain would preferentially see shower and thunderstorm development. A weak moisture gradient set up across northeast Utah and northwest Colorado during the afternoon, providing an additional focus for instability and lift, and it was this gradient that eventually spawned a stronger storm capable of producing heavy rainfall and a debris flow in Rio Blanco County.
episodes.195753: A series of storms dropped copious amounts of rainfall across northern Alaska from August 15th through the 23rd.  This rainfall caused rapid rises on streams and rivers which resulted in localized flooding of low-lying areas along northern Interior rivers.
episodes.195767: Modest instability and downdraft CAPE near a sea breeze circulation led to thunderstorms developing and then capable of producing damaging wind gusts as a cold front pushed south along the coast.
episodes.195857: As mid-level troughing deepened over the East Coast U.S., it sent an associated frontal boundary into the Southeast US on August 19th and further into Central Florida on the 20th. With this frontal boundary, it supported showers and thunderstorm over the southeastern Florida metro and adjacent waters. Passing storms brought the threat for strong, gusty winds and waterspouts over the marine areas.
episodes.196079: An active upper level pattern with a series of shortwave troughs moving over the region throughout the course of the week produced several days of strong to severe thunderstorms over the region.
episodes.196116: Thunderstorms brought gusty winds to much of Utah and flash flooding to southern Utah.

A tornado developed over the Bear Lodge Mountains, about 8 miles south of Alva, and tracked east-southeast for about two and a half miles. Numerous pine trees were either uprooted or snapped in half along its path. The estimated damage width was over a quarter mile in some areas, although some of the damage on the southern edge of the tornado was more consistent with straight line winds. No damage to property was noted. The tornado was on the ground for approximately 10 minutes with a speed of about 15 to 20 mph. The tornado was rated as an EF-1 with estimated winds up to 110 mph.
A public report via mPING reported hail of 1 inch in diameter.

Colorado Department of Transportation reported Colorado State Highway 64 closed at mile marker 56, between Wray Gulch Road and Indian Valley, due to a mudslide. This was just north of White River City, or 18 miles west of the town of Meeker along Highway 64. The road remained closed for several hours while cleanup was undertaken. This stretch of Highway 64 runs along the base of a steep cliff, leaving it prone to debris and mudflows during intense, heavy rainfall events.

Nearly 5 inches of rain fell between August 15th through August 19th, as reported by the Dahl Creek precipitation gage. The Kobuk River at Kobuk responded by rising into town after the first crest on August 20th. Kobuk experienced water over roadways and beneath homes and some citizens were unable to vote due to the flooding. An additional 2 inches of rain fell between August 21st and 23rd, resulting in water once again rising into town.
